title: Rosh Hashanah: Hannah (1 Samuel 1)
hook: the haftarah tells of Hannah praying for a child, and being heard
tomorrow: Rosh Hashanah: the boy is heard (Genesis 21)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the three sounds of the shofar. Your line was a sigh and a sob. Did a hard moment get its sigh, and then a long breath? Today, a woman whose prayer the rabbis learned from, read on the new year. Day six hundred forty-seven.

Every year, the family goes up to the sanctuary at Shiloh. Every year, there's a festive meal. And every year, the same scene. Elkanah gives portions of meat to his wife Peninnah and all her sons and daughters. To his other wife, Hannah, whom he loves, he gives a double portion. Because Hannah has no children. And Peninnah, every year, makes sure she feels it. Hannah cries and won't eat. Her husband asks, gently and a bit cluelessly: "am not I better to thee than ten sons?"
screen: `EVERY YEAR, UP TO SHILOH.` → `A DOUBLE PORTION, NO CHILDREN.` → `BETTER THAN TEN SONS?`

segments.voice: This is the haftarah, the prophetic reading, for the first day of Rosh Hashanah: the first chapter of the book of Samuel. Weeks ago we met Hannah's quiet prayer, the lips moving with no voice, which the rabbis made the model for the Amidah. Today, the question is why her story is read on the new year. The Talmud, in Rosh Hashanah 11a, says that on Rosh Hashanah three women were remembered: Sarah, Rachel and Hannah. Three women who had longed for children, and on this day, the tradition says, God remembered them. So on the day the liturgy is full of remembrance, the reading is about a woman who asked to be remembered, almost in those words. Her vow says: if Thou wilt "remember me, and not forget Thy handmaid." Watch what Hannah does in the story. She doesn't argue with Peninnah. She doesn't accept her husband's comfort as an answer. She gets up from the table, goes to the sanctuary, and pours out her soul. And when the priest Eli thinks she's drunk, she corrects him, respectfully and firmly. He blesses her. The text says her face was no more sad. Before anything has changed, she's already lighter. In time, she has a son, Samuel. And here's the turn: she gives him back, bringing him to serve at Shiloh. The next chapter is her song of thanks. It's about reversals: the Lord brings low and lifts up, the barren bears seven. Being heard, for Hannah, began before the answer came. It began with being seen.
screen: `THE FIRST DAY'S HAFTARAH.` · `SARAH, RACHEL AND HANNAH.` · `REMEMBER ME, AND NOT FORGET.` · `HER FACE WAS NO MORE SAD.` · then, large: `HANNAH WAS HEARD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name something you long for. Not a small want. Something you've carried, maybe for years, maybe quietly. Let yourself name it, the way Hannah got up from the table and named hers. If you pray, you can pour it out to God in your own words, silently, lips moving if you like. If you don't, say it to yourself, honestly, without needing an answer. Then notice whether naming it changes how you sit. The bell holds the time.
Rosh Hashanah. The new year, when the first day's reading tells of Hannah, remembered and heard.
Your line: Hannah was heard. Today, really listen to someone who's hurting, the way Eli finally did, and tell them what you heard. Day six hundred forty-seven.

screen: `DAY 647 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: ROSH HASHANAH: THE BOY IS HEARD (GENESIS 21).`

howItsDone: On the first day of Rosh Hashanah, after the Torah reading, the haftarah from 1 Samuel 1:1–2:10 is chanted in the synagogue, including Hannah's prayer and her song of thanks.

original.note: Hebrew: Hannah, a name from the root for grace and favor.

trapdoor: what you thought: a sad story about a woman who wanted a baby.
what it means: a woman who asked to be remembered, on the day of remembrance, and was seen before anything changed.
what a scholar hears: Rosh Hashanah 11a's three remembered women, Hannah's vow in 1 Samuel 1:11, and her song in chapter 2.

Editor review (y2 632–650): review overstated Hannah as "the model for all Jewish prayer"; now the rabbis learned from her prayer. "A year later" replaced by the text's "in time" (1 Samuel 1:20 does not say a year). Closing line no longer contradicts the story (she did receive a son).
